_meta.note: Every tunable number in the sim lives here. Code must never hardcode a balance figure. Each entry carries a `_comment` explaining what moving it does. Any balance change should ship with before/after `npm run simulate` output in the commit message.
_meta.phase: Phase 2 — named rival carriers share every market. The demand and share blocks were re-tuned when rivals arrived: see DECISIONS.md.

game._comment_startingCash: USD. Enough to lease a couple of narrowbodies and open a small network with runway to spare.
game._comment_horizonTurns: 100 quarters = 25 years. The victory check runs on the final turn.
game._comment_quartersPerYear: One turn = one quarter. Display only; the sim counts turns, never dates.
game._comment_startYear: Label for turn 0. Present-day start — there are no historical eras.
game._comment_corporateTaxRate: Tax on a profitable quarter. Airlines pay it and the model did not, so every dollar earned compounded straight back into the balance sheet. Losses are not carried forward yet — see DECISIONS.md.
game._comment_startingFuelPricePerL: USD per liter of jet fuel. Fixed in Phase 1; Phase 3 turns this into a random walk with event shocks.

routes._comment_openingCost: USD one-off to open a sector between two cities this carrier ALREADY serves: slot pair and launch marketing, nothing more. The station cost is charged separately per new city — see newStationCost.
routes._comment_newStationCost: USD one-off per ENDPOINT the carrier does not already serve (its home base always counts as served): hiring and training the station staff, the initial marketing, the deposits. Deliberately modest, because the standing cost of a station is carried by stationQuarterlyCost instead. This started at 6000000, doing the whole job on its own, and was cut when the ongoing charge was added: a one-off is a sunk cost the instant it is paid, so it can deter an opening but exerts no pressure afterwards, and a carrier sitting on forty thin stations felt nothing. It was also charging base prices for what is usually just a destination — outsourced handling and a station manager — when the genuinely expensive thing is a crewed base.
routes._comment_minDistanceKm: Below this, surface transport wins and the sector cannot be offered.
routes._comment_quarterlyFixedCost: USD per quarter for an active sector, on top of its share of the two stations it touches: its own slot pair and local selling, the part that genuinely scales per route rather than per station. Cut from 150000 when stationQuarterlyCost was introduced — most of what this used to stand for was station overhead being charged per route, which is why a network of forty single-sector stations cost the same per sector as a hub running six through one. Charged only when the sector has at least one in-range aircraft flying it.
routes._comment_stationQuarterlyCost: USD per quarter for each CITY the carrier operates, divided among its sectors touching that city — so a station carrying six sectors costs each of them a sixth. This is the ongoing half of what it means to hold a station: the manager, the staff, the handling contract, the office. It is the constant that makes density pay every quarter instead of once, and it is deliberately the larger of the two station figures: real stations cost far more to keep than to open, and the true penalty for a sprawling network is carrying overhead in forty places forever. Allocation is exact — a carrier pays this once per station however its sectors are arranged, so the split moves cost between sectors without inventing or losing any. Swept 0-1300000 on medium: the network keeps thickening all the way up (single-frame sectors 58% -> 46%, aircraft per sector 1.71 -> 2.20) but with clear diminishing returns past this point, and the world shrinks with it — 295 sectors a game down to 211. 600000 was taken as the last figure that buys most of the shape change while leaving the map populated, and $2.4M a year is a defensible cost for a mainline station. Note it also has to be roughly this large to bite at all: the one-off it replaced was $6M, which the AI amortises over an 8-quarter horizon into $750K a quarter of deterrent, so anything under about $375K per station is a weaker signal than what came before it.
routes._comment_maxAircraftPerRoute: Caps how hard one city pair can be farmed; forces network breadth.
routes._comment_commitmentQuarters: How long an AI carrier sticks with a sector it has just opened before it will close it for losing money — a route ramp-up period. Real airlines give a new route 18-24 months to mature and will eat losses to build share in a market they have decided to contest. Without this the AI closed any route that printed one negative quarter, so a rival entering the player's market was squeezed out within a quarter or two and competition never lasted long enough to hurt: the player won every war of attrition by default. A committed carrier keeps its capacity in the market, which drags the incumbent's load factor down for years. Scaled by the difficulty `contestPressure` mod, so rivals on hard dig in far longer than on easy. A carrier below its cash reserve still retreats regardless — commitment is not a suicide pact.

demand._comment_populationExponent: Exponent on each city population in the gravity product. Well below 1 on purpose: with linear population, big-city pairs dominate the map by two orders of magnitude more than real traffic does. Raise it to make megacities matter more, at the cost of flattening the rest of the world into unflyable markets.
demand._comment_k: Gravity scale. baseDemand = k * (popA*wA)*(popB*wB) / dist^exponent. Turn this to move the whole world's demand up or down; watch load factors in headless.
demand._comment_weightExponent: How strongly economic weight scales market size, as pop*weight^exponent. Sub-1 keeps lower-income regions from having markets too thin to fly at all.
demand._comment_distanceExponent: How fast demand falls with distance. Higher = short-haul-heavy world; lower = long-haul matters more.
demand._comment_longHaulDecayStartKm: Distance beyond which an extra exponential decay kicks in, so ultra-long sectors stay thin.
demand._comment_longHaulDecayScaleKm: e-folding distance of that decay. Larger = gentler long-haul falloff.
demand._comment_maxLoadFactor: BASELINE ceiling on the share of offered seats that can be sold on a sector turning traffic away — what a carrier can fill on a GOOD route in an AVERAGE quarter, not what its network averages over a year. Those are different numbers and conflating them is the trap here: published industry load factor of 82-84% is an average over full and empty flights, so the ceiling belongs ABOVE it. 88% is a full-service carrier's strong routes; Ryanair sustains 94-95% system-wide, which is why the hard cap sits at 94. What pulls the network average below the ceiling is seasonality (see `seasonality`) and day-of-week and directional peaking, which are demand-side and must not be smuggled in here — this number is a supply-side limit. Without any ceiling every strong route flies 100% full, inflating RASK about 20% against a realistic CASK. A baseline, not a constant: revenue management, capacity planning and repeat custom all raise it.
demand._comment_loadCeilingMax: Hard cap however much a carrier invests. Nobody sells the last seat on every departure.
demand._comment_elasticityLeisure: Price elasticity of demand on a pure-leisure route, as a positive magnitude. Gillen/InterVISTAS put leisure near -1.9 (a 10% fare cut brings ~19% more traffic) against about -0.5 for business. A carrier's captured demand is stimulated by (its posture fare / match fare)^(-elasticity): undercutting a leisure market pulls in price-sensitive travellers who would not fly at full fare, premium pricing drives them off. This is real NEW demand the discounter captures, not share stolen from rivals — see DECISIONS.md. Raising it makes low-cost, high-density flying dramatically stronger on holiday routes.
demand._comment_elasticityBusiness: Price elasticity on a pure-business route. Business travellers barely move on price (fare is a small part of a business trip's cost), so undercutting a Zurich or Frankfurt market fills far fewer incremental seats than undercutting Cancun. Between the two anchors the route's elasticity interpolates on its combined city weight.
demand._comment_leisureWeightBelow: Combined route weight sqrt(wA*wB) at or below which a market is treated as fully leisure (elasticityLeisure). City weight is business-travel intensity, so low-weight pairs are holiday markets. 0.6 is roughly the 10th percentile of route weight.
demand._comment_businessWeightAbove: Combined route weight at or above which a market is fully business (elasticityBusiness). ~90th percentile. Between this and leisureWeightBelow the elasticity interpolates linearly.
demand._comment_noiseStdDev: Std dev of the per-market, per-quarter multiplicative demand shock. Drawn once per city pair, so two carriers sharing a market always see the same quarter as each other.
demand._comment_seasonality: How demand moves around the year. This is what turns `maxLoadFactor` back into a ceiling rather than a level: without it every strong sector sits pinned at the same load factor in every quarter forever.

seasonality._comment_index: Demand by quarter of the year at a fully seasonal latitude, as a multiplier on the annual mean. MUST average to 1.0 across the four entries, or the world's demand changes as well as its shape. Q3/Q1 of 1.35 matches the North Atlantic summer peak against the February trough. This is the mechanism `maxLoadFactor` used to stand in for: real published load factor of 83% is an average over a full July and a half-empty February, not a level anyone flies at all year.
seasonality._comment_tropicLatitudeDeg: Below this latitude a city has no seasonal swing at all. Tropical markets really are close to flat; Singapore does not have a summer.
seasonality._comment_fullEffectLatitudeDeg: At and above this latitude a city gets the full swing in `index`, ramping linearly from the tropic. Southern-hemisphere cities get the same curve with the peak moved half a year, so a Sydney carrier's good quarter is a London carrier's bad one.

demand._comment_departureKFactor: Coefficient of variation of demand for a single DEPARTURE — the industry K-factor. Demand is not a number, it is a distribution: some departures go out full and others half empty, and that variance is the entire reason a real network averages 82-84% load factor rather than the high 90s. Load factor is then an OUTCOME of how well capacity matches uncertain demand (see expectedLoad in demand.ts), not a ceiling anyone has to justify. MIT 16.75J uses 0.35; market studies report up to ~0.48. Lower it and departures become predictable, so a carrier can size closer to the mean and fill more of the aeroplane — which is exactly what revenue management buys, and is how the revenue-management technology programs are modelled.

fare._comment_base: USD fixed component of a one-way fare (booking, taxes floor).
fare._comment_perKm: USD per km before the sublinear distance curve is applied.
fare._comment_distanceExponent: Sub-1 so per-km yield declines with distance: long-haul fares grow slower than distance. These three numbers were fitted by least squares to published yield per km — roughly 17 cents short-haul, 10.5 medium, 7 long-haul — rather than tuned by feel; the fit lands within about 5% across the whole distance range. Refit them together, not one at a time. Too low and long-haul cannot cover its costs; too high and short-haul becomes a license to print money.
fare._comment_fuelPassThrough: How much of a fuel price move the industry passes into fares — the surcharge effect. Every carrier faces the same fuel bill, so when it rises they all reprice. Without this a fuel spike is unsurvivable: costs move and fares do not, and two thirds of well-run airlines go under. Below 1 on purpose, so a spike still hurts; you recover only part of it. It keys off the SPOT price, not your hedged price, because the market reprices on what everyone pays — which is exactly what makes a hedge valuable.
fare._comment_weightExponent: How strongly city economic weight lifts fares, as (wA*wB)^(exponent/2). Keep this well below 1: weight already scales market size through the gravity model, so a high value double-counts it and makes low-weight regions unflyable while rich ones run away.
fare._comment_monopolyPremium: Extra yield a carrier earns on an UNCONTESTED route, as a fraction added to the base competitive fare. A route no rival serves clears at (1 + this) times the fare; the premium decays toward the base fare as rivals add capacity (see competitionHalfShare). Grounded in real data: DOT airfare reports show the least-competitive routes carry the highest fares, and competitive entry compresses yields 15-25% (MIT: an LCC entry cuts fares ~8%, a ULCC ~21%; Southwest's entry averaged -15%, up to -32% at MSP). Southwest flies ~60% of its network with no direct competitor, which is exactly what sustains small aircraft on thin routes. Without this the sim gives a vacant route the same fare as a five-carrier dogfight, so a monopolist cannot price to cover a high-unit-cost turboprop and small aircraft are unprofitable everywhere. 0.28 is mid-band of the observed monopoly premium. Too high and uncontested flying prints money; too low and small gauges stay dead content.
fare._comment_competitionHalfShare: Rival scheduled capacity, as a fraction of the market's weekly demand, at which the monopoly premium is halved. premium = monopolyPremium / (1 + rivalShare/this). Small so the FIRST entrant compresses yield the most, matching the real Southwest effect where one low-cost entrant cuts fares 15-21% and further entrants matter less. Raise it to make competition erode fares more slowly (pricing power lingers); lower it to make a single rival gut the premium.

share._comment_gaugeElasticity: The S-curve: market share tracks CAPACITY share, not just frequency. A carrier offering more seats per departure wins more share, holding frequency equal — real airlines gain share 'whether from a larger proportion of smaller aircraft or a smaller proportion of larger ones' (ScienceDirect, s-curve vs schedule-delay). Kept well below 1, and frequency kept sublinear too, so neither piling frequency nor upgauging onto one trunk route runs away — the empirical curve is closer to linear than to a dramatic S, and chasing it is what causes real-world overcapacity. Set to 0 to price gauge out of share entirely.
share._comment_refSeatsPerDeparture: Seats-per-departure that counts as neutral gauge (an A320-class narrowbody). Attractiveness scales with (seatsPerDeparture / this)^gaugeElasticity, so a 325-seat widebody is worth about (325/180)^0.4 = 1.26x a ref aircraft on the same frequency, and a 76-seat turboprop about 0.72x. Only the ratio matters, so moving this rescales nothing on its own — it just re-centres which aircraft is 'neutral'.
share._comment_frequencyElasticity: Attractiveness ~ (round-trips/week)^elasticity. ABOVE 1, so the curve is convex: a carrier with more capacity on a market wins MORE than proportional traffic. That is the S-curve, the central empirical regularity of airline competition and the reason carriers fight over frequency on a route. This was 0.62 — below 1, which inverts the curve and makes the bigger operator win LESS than its share of the seats. The damage was not mainly to competition between named carriers: it was that suppressing their pull left the AMBIENT incumbent (share.incumbentBase, the unmodelled rest of the industry) holding 54% of a solo market and 44% of a duopoly — more than either real carrier on it. Most of the competition in the game was a constant, which is why rivals felt weak, why adding metal did not pay, and why nobody could ever be muscled off a route: you cannot out-compete a constant. At 1.15 the ambient share of a duopoly falls to 11%, aircraft per sector rise 1.68 -> 1.94, and no pile-on appears (the per-route aircraft cap already bound at every value tested). Chosen over 1.30 because it keeps nearly all of the correction for less of the side effect; the published curve sits nearer 1.3-1.7, and going that far is defensible only once slot scarcity exists to check it. NOTE this makes the game EASIER on its own — the player was paying the same phantom tax and gets it back too — so difficulty has to be won back separately rather than by walking this number down again. TESTED AT 1.15 AND REVERTED, 2026-08-07 — the diagnosis behind the experiment holds and the fix does not. Above 1 the curve is convex, which is the real S-curve, and it does what was wanted: the ambient incumbent (share.incumbentBase) falls from 48% of a duopoly to 11%, carrier share rises 21% -> 45%, and aircraft per sector rise 1.68 -> 1.94 without any pile-on. It also breaks the gauge decision. On a thin sector the widebody goes from -$0.65M to +$2.30M and beats the correctly sized aeroplane, because the phantom was what kept large types half empty. Lowering incumbentBase directly hits the SAME wall at the same place: right-sizing fails once a carrier wins more than roughly 25-30% of a market, whichever lever takes it there. So the gauge decision currently works BECAUSE most of the market is held by a constant, and fixing the constant needs right-sizing restored by other means — short-sector penalties on large types, a gauge-sensitive load ceiling, or a wider gap between the frequency and gauge exponents. That is a recalibration, not a knob turn.
share._comment_incumbentBase: Ambient competition strength. This is the passive 'demand sink' — the rest of the industry the player splits every market with. Higher = harder to win share. Phase 2 added named rivals, so this was cut from 0.18 to 0.10: it now represents only the small operators the game does not model, leaving room for named carriers to actually bite. Raising it back makes rivals irrelevant.
share._comment_competitionLoadPenalty: How much rival capacity on a market erodes EVERYONE'S achievable load factor — overcapacity biting load, not just fare. Trunk markets are so large against a few aircraft that a lone entrant never dents the incumbent's traffic (it just fills from the huge spill), so competition used to be invisible except as a small fare dip. This makes a contested route fly emptier: the load ceiling is scaled by (1 - penalty * rivalCapacityShare), where rivalCapacityShare is rivals' seats / all seats on the market. One equal rival (share 0.5) takes an 88% monopoly route to ~70%; a crowd craters it. Realistic — contested routes really do run lower load factors as carriers over-schedule to hold share. This is the main thing that makes a competitor's ENTRY felt. 0 restores the old fare-only competition.
share._comment_incumbentDemandExponent: How incumbent strength scales with market size, so big markets aren't trivially captured by one plane.
share._comment_spillCapture: How much of a turned-away passenger re-books with a carrier that still has a seat, rather than not travelling at all. Spill used to be deleted outright, which made under-capacity free: nobody gained from your shortfall, so the profit-maximal build always sat under demand and load factor pinned to the ceiling on ~88% of sector-quarters (docs/demand-audit.md). At 1 every turned-away passenger re-books somewhere; at 0 the old behaviour returns. 0.6 says most people find another seat and some give up.

feed._comment: The hub-connectivity bonus (CLAUDE.md §6). A carrier that already flies many routes touching a sector's endpoints wins more share on it — connecting traffic funnels through a hub — so a network is worth more than the sum of its point-to-point routes. It scores the OTHER routes the carrier flies at each endpoint (never itineraries, per the v1 non-goal), and multiplies that carrier's attractiveness in the share split. This is what gives the fortress-hub and legacy archetypes a real mechanical edge, and what lets a small aircraft earn its keep as a feeder into a hub rather than only on its standalone P&L.
feed._comment_maxBonus: The largest attractiveness uplift a fully-built hub confers, as a fraction. A carrier with no other routes at either endpoint gets nothing; a dominant hub approaches this ceiling. Kept moderate and capped so a hub carrier does not snowball into owning the map — watch the 'no carrier owns the world' regression invariant when moving it.
feed._comment_halfRoutes: Connecting routes (other sectors the carrier flies touching the two endpoints, summed) at which the bonus reaches half its ceiling: bonus = maxBonus * n / (n + this). Saturating, so the first few feeder routes matter most and a giant hub does not run away. Lower makes a modest network feel like a hub sooner.

events._comment_chancePerQuarter: Odds a new card is drawn in a given quarter. At most one event starts at a time so the board can tell what hit it; two simultaneous shocks read as noise.
events._comment_fuelVolatility: Std dev of the quarterly log move in the fuel price. Real jet fuel moves this much and more; this is the main thing that stops a well-run airline's income being a straight line.
events._comment_fuelReversion: How strongly the fuel price is pulled back to its long-run level each quarter. A plain random walk eventually wanders somewhere absurd over a hundred quarters.
events._comment_fuelPriceMin: Floor on the walk, USD per liter. Roughly the cheapest crude has traded.
events._comment_fuelPriceMax: Ceiling on the walk, USD per liter. Roughly the dearest crude has traded.
events._comment_completionMean: Baseline share of the schedule that operates. Airlines cancel a small slice every quarter to weather, technical faults and air traffic control.
events._comment_completionStdDev: Quarter-to-quarter variation in that share. This is the only source of variance that reaches a sold-out sector, because it removes seats rather than passengers — a demand shock on a spilling route just spills less.
events._comment_completionFloor: Worst the baseline can get before events are applied.
events._comment_hedgeMaxFraction: Most of next year's fuel a carrier may lock forward. Never all of it — nobody hedges 100%.
events._comment_hedgeWhenBelow: Fraction of the long-run fuel price below which an AI carrier will lock forward. Set low on purpose: a hedge is a genuine gamble, not free insurance. It costs a premium over spot, and because the industry fare surcharge tracks SPOT, a carrier that locks in and then watches fuel fall pays the high price while fares drop around it. Airlines have lost fortunes doing this. At 0.95 the fixture hedged so often it measurably hurt itself.
events._comment_hedgeQuarters: How far forward a hedge runs.
events._comment_hedgePremium: What the counterparty charges over spot to take the risk. Above 1, so hedging is insurance rather than free money — it costs a little on average and pays off when fuel spikes.

posture._comment: The things a pricing posture changes, kept together because they only make sense as a set. Posture is a cabin decision as much as a price one: a premium carrier fits fewer, better seats and sells them dearer; a low-cost carrier crams more in and sells them cheap. FIVE notches, not three. The three originals keep their exact figures so a saved route still means what it meant, and one was added at each end: SKIM, for a monopoly turning away more passengers than it carries at the old ceiling, and STIMULATE, for growing a market that is thinner than the metal on it. Every column is monotonic across the five — that is the invariant a new notch must not break.
posture._comment_seats: Seat count multiplier on the aircraft's baseline. This is real and large: the same narrowbody carries about 160 seats in a legacy config with a business cabin and about 190 in a low-cost one. It means premium trades capacity for yield and undercut does the reverse, so the better posture depends on whether the sector is short of seats or short of passengers.
posture._comment_fare: Revenue per seat. Premium is well above the old 1.18 because a premium cabin is not a surcharge on the same seat — it is a different, far dearer product sold in place of several economy seats.
posture._comment_paxCost: Multiplier on the per-passenger cost. This is what stops premium being a cheat code: a business cabin is genuinely expensive to serve — catering, lounges, more cabin crew per passenger, corporate distribution — while a no-frills carrier spends almost nothing per head. Without it, premium raises fares on a sold-out sector for free, because the share it sheds was being spilled anyway. SOFTENING THIS WAS TRIED AND REVERTED on 2026-08-13 — see DECISIONS.md. The short answer: the spread is load-bearing. Swept as 1+(old-1)*k, the number of distinct best postures across sector lengths holds at three down to k=0.7 and collapses at k=0.6, but the SUITE disagrees with that reading — k=0.7 kills two of six history worlds and breaks the posture-shape test at 720km, and k=0.9 tripped a latent quote-vs-charge bug in the acquisition path, since FIXED (stale fleet book value cache — see DECISIONS.md 2026-08-13). A retune is now unblocked, but it must be swept across MORE than one fleet size and must include the history scenario: the sweep that produced k=0.7 used six routes at one fleet size on `present` only, and missed both regressions.
posture._comment_attractiveness: Share of the market the posture wins. Undercut pulls traffic, premium sheds it.

fleet._comment_utilizationHoursPerDay: Block hours per aircraft per day available for rotations. Drives derived frequency.
fleet._comment_blockPadHoursPerLeg: Taxi, climb and descent overhead added to each one-way leg's cruise time.
fleet._comment_handlingPerDeparture: USD per departure, flat part: ground handling, gate, dispatch.
fleet._comment_handlingPerSeat: USD per departure per seat of gauge: landing and navigation charges scale with aircraft size, so a widebody turn costs far more than a turboprop turn. NOTE: this split charges a 72-seat turboprop $20.67 a seat against a widebody's $6.50, which is why handling is the largest single cost line on a regional sector (29% of revenue) and no turboprop route is profitable anywhere on the map. Reshaping it was tried and is NOT a drive-by change — see DECISIONS.md, 2026-08-02.
fleet._comment_overheadRate: Corporate overhead as an uplift on a sector's operating costs: head office, IT, sales, scheduling, admin. Real airlines run 10-15% of operating expense here and it is inside every published CASM figure, but the model had no line for it at all — which is why modeled CASK came out about 15% below the real benchmark for medium-haul narrowbody flying.
fleet._comment_costWeightExponent: How strongly city economic weight scales the LOCAL cost lines (crew, ground handling), as (wA*wB)^(exponent/2). Fuel and lease rates are world prices and are deliberately excluded. Without this the model charges New York labor rates in Delhi while also suppressing Delhi fares, which made low-income regions unflyable at any gauge or load factor. Keep it EQUAL to fare.weightExponent so the local-cost portion is margin-neutral.
fleet._comment_distributionPerPax: USD per passenger carried, covering everything that scales with traffic rather than capacity: booking and distribution, catering and in-flight service, passenger ground handling. Fitted so ASK-weighted CASK lands mid-band against published CASM. It was 8 while only distribution was modeled, which left costs about 20% light.
fleet._comment_standingCostPerSeatQuarter: USD per quarter per SEAT of gauge, owed whether the aircraft flies or not (insurance, admin, parking). Per-seat rather than flat: a flat charge taxed a 48-seat turboprop the same as a 480-seat quad and left the small end of the fleet ladder with no niche at all. Makes idle aircraft bleed cash in proportion to their size.
fleet._comment_depreciationPerQuarter: Share of an owned aircraft's book value it loses each quarter (1.8%/qtr = ~7%/yr, a ~25-year life to a modest residual). Does two jobs, both real: it writes the asset down on the balance sheet (so net worth reflects a wasting asset), and it is charged to the SECTOR as the ownership cost of owned metal — exactly the 'Depreciation' line on a real airline income statement, the owned-aircraft counterpart to the rent a leased one pays. It is a non-cash charge: the purchase was paid up front, so it never touches the cash that drives bankruptcy. Because it is charged on book value, an older owned aircraft costs less to own and more to maintain — as in reality.
fleet._comment_saleValueFraction: Fraction of current book value recovered when selling an owned aircraft.
fleet._comment_maintAgeSaturationYears: e-folding age of the maintenance curve. Cost approaches base + maintAgeSlope*saturationYears rather than rising for ever, so an old airframe is expensive but not unboundedly so. A straight line here bankrupts any carrier that holds a fleet two decades.
fleet._comment_leaseTermYears: Lease commitment. Handing an aircraft back inside the term costs the break fee below. Without a term, resetting an airframe's age costs only the deposit and leasing strictly dominates owning.
fleet._comment_leaseBreakFraction: Share of the remaining lease owed when returning early. 0 makes leases free to churn; 1 makes them impossible to exit.
fleet._comment_overhaulCostFraction: Cost of a heavy maintenance visit on an OWNED aircraft, as a fraction of list price. Resets the airframe's effective age. This is the owner's answer to aging — without it, owning is a one-way bet against the maintenance curve. Tune so it is situational: too dear and nobody ever overhauls, too cheap and it is automatic.
fleet._comment_deliveryQuartersByKlass: Quarters between ordering an aircraft (leased or bought) and it entering service. Real backlogs run 10-14 years; compressed here to keep a 100-turn game moving, but the principle holds — you commit capital ahead of the market and cannot grow instantly. Bigger metal takes longer. Turboprops arrive next quarter so the very first turn still gets an aircraft flying soon.
fleet._comment_leaseDepositMonths: Months of lease charged up front on signing, as cash out.
fleet._comment_offMakerCostPenalty: Extra crew and maintenance cost an airline pays to operate an aircraft from outside the manufacturer it is built around, as a fraction. Fleet commonality is worth real money — one type rating, one spares pool, one set of procedures — which is why carriers in life are Boeing shops or Airbus shops rather than picking the marginally better aircraft each time. Without it every carrier ran the same appraisal and reached the same answer: measured, one type was 53.5% of all aircraft-quarters and a carrier's fleet was a median 86% a single type, but they were all the SAME single type. Only applies to the two full-line makers (Aros and Vanta); the niche builders are bought for jobs nobody else covers, so there is no commonality to lose.

cargo._comment: Belly freight. A widebody's lower deck is a second business, and it is the main reason a real airline puts one on a long thin route: the hold fills whether or not the cabin does. Modelled per AVAILABLE seat-km rather than as a share of passenger revenue, because cargo is capacity-driven, not passenger-driven — a half-empty cabin still flies a full belly, and it is precisely that independence that makes the widebody worth flying.
cargo._comment_revenuePerSeatKm: USD earned per available seat-km of the aircraft's BASE gauge (a proxy for hold volume). Anchored on the published transatlantic figure: a FULL widebody belly earns $40-80k a flight at $2-4/kg. The dial is hold utilisation, and it must be the INDUSTRY AVERAGE, not the trunk-route figure, because one rate here applies to every widebody sector including thin ones that would never fill a hold. IATA's busiest corridors run 67.5% and 61.4% cargo load factor; the industry as a whole sits near 50%, and 50% is what this uses: 0.012 * 365 * 6000 = ~$26k on a transatlantic twin, about 17% of that flight's passenger revenue. Calibrating on the trunk figure instead (0.016, ~23%) made the whole world richer than it should be and collapsed the outcome spread the Phase 3 acceptance test measures. Narrowbody holds are bulk-loaded and mostly baggage, so they earn about an eighth of the rate per seat; regional aircraft earn nothing worth modelling. NOTE the share of revenue RISES with distance on its own, because this is linear in distance while fares are sub-linear (fare.distanceExponent) — the real pattern, and it needs no extra constant.

stubAi._comment: The headless balance fixture that stands in for a player. Not a rival — rivals are configured in archetypes.json. Used by the headless runner and the CI regression suite. It matches aircraft gauge to market size by probing the route economics, and only commits to sectors that project profitable. It is a fixture for balance, not a designed rival: if a competent operator cannot make money with it, the economy is wrong — the archetypes arrive in Phase 2.
stubAi._comment_fortressHub: The fixture only opens sectors touching its home city. Point-to-point growth from every city it serves compounds into a hundred-route network and stops being a useful balance yardstick.
stubAi._comment_maxOrigins: Hubs considered when opening. Only matters for a non-fortress carrier; searching from every city it serves is the most expensive thing an AI turn does.
stubAi._comment_incursionShortlist: Rival markets examined for a possible incursion, richest first.
stubAi._comment_incursionAppetite: The fixture will contest a market a rival has proven. Without this it only ever opens virgin sectors while rivals raid it freely, and it stops being a fair yardstick for what a competent player can do.
stubAi._comment_techAboveCash: Cash an AI carrier keeps free before funding a technology program. Tech is a permanent margin improvement but the money is gone for several quarters before anything lands, so it is only sane when the balance sheet is comfortable.
stubAi._comment_growthDrag: How much each existing sector raises the cash bar for opening another, so the fixture decelerates as it grows instead of compounding.

ai._comment: Behaviour shared by the archetype rivals (not the stub fixture, which stays a conservative baseline for balance measurement).
ai._comment_borrowFraction: Fraction of remaining borrowing capacity a profitable rival draws to fund expansion. Half, to keep headroom against a bad quarter rather than max-levering.
ai._comment_borrowMin: A rival will not bother borrowing less than this.
ai._comment_appraisalQuarters: The planning horizon a carrier judges an INVESTMENT over — opening a sector, contesting one, adding an aircraft. Two years. Across it, fuel is assumed to revert toward its long-run level and a running shock is counted only for the quarters it has left, so the decision is priced on the cycle rather than the bottom of it. Decisions about REALITY — closing a loss-maker, retreating when cash runs short — deliberately still use today's actual conditions, because that is what the bank sees. Before this, every rival decision hung on a single quarter's cash at today's spot fuel: they piled into markets during a glut and abandoned them when it passed, churn that read as stupidity rather than strategy. Longer makes carriers look further through a spike and commit more readily; at 1 they are back to judging a fifteen-year aircraft on this quarter's fuel price.
ai._comment_capitalPerGrowthMove: USD of deployable cash a carrier reckons one growth move commits — a sector plus the aeroplane to fly it. Deliberately a NOTIONAL capital figure rather than the cash a move actually takes out of the bank, because leasing costs only a deposit while buying costs the whole price: budgeting on cash out of the door would let a carrier lease its way to twenty sectors in a quarter on the same balance sheet. Measured against this, expansion is limited by the money behind it rather than by a quota of decisions. Raise it to make carriers hoard; lower it to make them deploy harder.
ai._comment_maxGrowthMovesPerQuarter: Hard ceiling on growth moves in one quarter, whatever the balance sheet says. Not a balance figure — a backstop, so a pathological cash pile cannot turn one turn into a hundred route openings and so the loop can never run away. If this is ever the binding constraint in ordinary play, capitalPerGrowthMove is set too low.
ai._comment_cornerPull: How much more a Territorial values a sector touching its own hub. Applied as willingness — it lifts a positive projection and softens a negative one — rather than as a multiplier on the figure, because a thin sector often appraises negative and multiplying THAT by a bigger appetite would make the most territorial carrier avoid its own city hardest. That trap is documented on bestIncursion's playerFocus and it is the same one. Swept 1.9/3.0/4.5/7.0 on the share of a Territorial's network that touches its own hub and the share of that hub it ends up holding: 36%/50%, 43%/58%, 53%/68%, 47%/74%. 4.5 is where concentration peaks — past it the carrier takes so much of its own city that it runs out of sectors there and spreads again, and more of them go under paying over the odds (13 survivors at 1.9 against 10 at 7.0), which is the intended fragility but not to the point of the archetype never being seen.
ai._comment_cornerRentThreshold: Share of a hub's sectors a Territorial must hold before it stops matching and starts charging premium there. Below it the set is unfinished and a premium fare just hands share to whoever else is standing on the market; above it the city is effectively its own and the fare is what the whole exercise was for. This is the beat that makes the archetype read as the board game rather than as one more expansionist. Lowered 0.55 -> 0.45 on 2026-08-07 because the funded growth allowance made every carrier deploy cash as fast as it earns it, so hubs are contested harder and a Territorial's median dominance now settles around 44% — under the old bar, meaning the rent almost never fired. Swept 0.55/0.45/0.38/0.30/0.24 over 16 seeds on the share of its own hub's sectors it prices premium, against a legacy carrier, and on how many Territorials survive: 17%/49%/84%/97%/98% against legacy 11%/13%/22%/11%/10%, with 14/12/10/9/8 survivors. 0.45 is the pick. 0.38 and below invert the thing the archetype is FOR — at 0.38 the legacy carrier ends up holding more of its hub (60% against 53%) because the Territorial prices itself off its own city — and by 0.30 nearly every home sector is premium, which is a constant rather than a decision. At 0.45 the rent fires on about half its home network, which reads as a carrier choosing its moment.
ai._comment_cornerDefence: How much harder a Territorial goes after a market flown out of a city it is trying to own, whoever is flying it. This is the half that makes a hub feel OWNED rather than merely busy: open a sector out of a Territorial's home and it turns up on one of yours, which is the behaviour the roster was missing. Higher than playerFocus on medium because it is not about the player — it is about the city.
ai._comment_trunkMarkets: How many of the world's richest city pairs every carrier considers, on top of the routes touching its own hubs. Route discovery used to be entirely hub-anchored, which meant the biggest markets on the map went unflown unless a carrier happened to be based on one, and markets almost never held more than one carrier because so few carriers could see any given one. This is the list everybody watches. Raise it for a more crowded, more contested world; 0 restores purely hub-anchored planning.

finance._comment: Phase 4: the financial layer. Share price, debt, equity and acquisitions. Modeled on Railroad Tycoon: bonds priced by credit rating, buy/issue stock, become majority owner then buy out the rest.
finance._comment_startingShares: Shares every carrier floats at the start. Only ratios matter (price = equity / shares), so the absolute number is cosmetic — it sets the order of magnitude of the share price.
finance._comment_peMultiple: Price/earnings multiple applied to trailing-year earnings when valuing a carrier above its book value. Real airlines trade around 6-12x. Market cap = book value + peMultiple x max(0, trailing earnings) x growth.
finance._comment_growth: The earnings multiple is scaled by a growth factor in [floor, cap] from how this year's earnings compare with last year's. A fast grower is worth more than its trailing earnings imply; a shrinker less.
finance._comment_equityRaiseDiscount: Where a SMALL issue clears, as a fraction of the market price. The real discount widens with the size of the raise — see equityRaiseDepthPenalty — because a buyer has to be found for every share and a large block only clears if it is priced to move. This was a flat 0.93 whatever the size, which meant a 1% top-up and a raise of a quarter of the company both cleared at the same price and a company-rescuing issue moved the share price by 1.5%. Rights issues at that scale price far below market in life, and that is the entire reason boards hesitate before one.
finance._comment_equityRaiseDepthPenalty: How much further below market the issue clears per unit of market cap raised. At 0.6, a 5% raise clears near 94% of market and a 25% raise near 82% — the difference between a top-up and a rescue. This is the constant that makes issuing equity a decision with a cost rather than a button that prints money, and it is what stops the per-quarter ceiling being the only thing a player weighs.
finance._comment_equityRaiseFloorPrice: Hard floor on the issue price as a fraction of market, so an enormous raise against a tiny market cap cannot price at nothing and mint unbounded shares.
finance._comment_maxEquityRaiseFraction: Most of its own value a carrier may raise in new equity in one go. Stops a carrier printing unlimited shares in a turn.
finance._comment_authorizedIssuanceFraction: The authorized-share ceiling. Cumulative equity issuance (split-adjusted) may not exceed this fraction of a carrier's float, so over a whole game a carrier can grow its share count by at most ~f/(1-f) = 67% through issuance. This is the real-world charter limit: a company cannot print shares without bound, and past the authorized cap it would need a shareholder vote. Issuing raises real cash but is a FINITE well — it stops equity issuance being an endless market-cap pump, and it makes a raided board's defensive dilution run out (a determined raider eventually overwhelms it). Lower makes equity scarcer and takeovers easier to finish.
finance._comment_interestByRating: QUARTERLY interest rate on outstanding debt, by credit rating. ~4-23% annualized. A poor rating makes debt a trap, exactly as in Railroad Tycoon — borrow cheap when strong, not dear when desperate.
finance._comment_leverageForRating: Upper bound on debt / assets for each rating. A carrier's rating is the best band its leverage fits within; losses drag it down one notch.
finance._comment_maxLeverage: Hard ceiling on debt / assets. A carrier cannot borrow past this, and crossing it (through asset loss) forces a rating to junk.
finance._comment_dividendDeduction: Share of a dividend RECEIVED from another carrier that escapes tax, by how much of the payer you own. Modelled on the US dividends-received deduction, which is the mechanism economists credit with killing the American pyramid rather than any single prohibition: a chain held at 51% is taxed at every layer on the way up, and only an 80%-plus holding files consolidated and passes cash untaxed. Thresholds in dividendDeductionBands. This is what makes control-on-51% cheap to BUILD and expensive to DRAIN, and it puts a real decision in front of a controller — stay at half and keep the capital free, or pay up past four fifths and stop leaking. Before it existed, cash cascading up a chain leaked to minority holders but not a cent to tax, so depth cost nothing.
finance._comment_dividendDeductionBands: Ownership fractions where the deduction steps up: below `affiliate` a holder is a minority investor, at or above `consolidated` it may file as one company. The real figures are 20% and 80% and they are used unchanged, because the 80% line is exactly what stops a 51% controller passing cash up untaxed and is the whole point of the mechanic.
finance._comment_subsidiaryReserve: USD a controlled carrier must be left holding when its controller pulls cash out of it. Looting a subsidiary is a real robber-baron move and is meant to be available — the 1990 Railroad Tycoon made a whole strategy of it — but a subsidiary stripped to nothing simply fails next quarter, which turns the mechanic into a way of deleting rivals rather than a way of financing yourself. The floor is what keeps it a financing decision.
finance._comment_subsidiaryTransferCapPerQuarter: Share of a controlled carrier's cash its controller may move in one quarter, in either direction. Without a cap the whole treasury moves on the turn control lands and the structure has no ongoing decision in it. Note the economics already price this without any help: cash sits in standaloneEquity, so pulling a dollar out of a subsidiary drops its equity by a dollar and your own holding by your share of that — you keep the dollar and the minority holders eat their fraction of the loss. That is exactly the historical trick and it needs bounding, not balancing.
finance._comment_minCarriersAfterMerger: Antitrust: an AI carrier will not complete an acquisition that would leave fewer than this many solvent carriers on the board — the competition authority blocks it, exactly as regulators block airline mergers that would gut a market. This is the backstop for the §9 invariant that no carrier runs away with the world. It became necessary once legacy and flag carriers turned acquisitive alongside the roll-up: over a 50-year history game consolidation snowballed, and one seed ended with a single survivor holding 100% of rival routes after 16 takeovers. Deliberately NOT applied to the player, whose own path to victory by clearing the board is a designed win condition — a player consolidating the industry is winning the game, an AI doing it is a broken world. Bankruptcies are unaffected; only mergers are reviewed.
finance._comment_greenmailPremium: What a carrier must pay, as a multiple of market value, to buy a single shareholder's whole stake in ITSELF and retire it — the classic greenmail payoff. Above acquisitionPremium on purpose: a raider who has you cornered knows you are the desperate party and prices accordingly. This is the surgical counter to a raid (the other being dilution by issuing equity), and it is deliberately expensive — it drains the cash that would otherwise buy aircraft, it lowers your market cap by what you paid, and retiring the shares shrinks your float, which RAISES every remaining holder's percentage and permanently reduces how much equity you may still issue. Nothing stops the same raider buying back in from the float later, at market, having sold to you at a premium — which is exactly the criticism greenmail attracted in the 1980s.
finance._comment_dominanceNoticedAbove: Share of the world's sectors a carrier may hold before the rest of the board starts treating it as the one to beat. Below this nothing changes. Set near a third because that is roughly where a carrier stops being one of several and becomes the market: it is a threshold for being NOTICED, not for winning.
finance._comment_dominancePressure: How hard the world pushes back per unit of share above the threshold. It raises what a dominant buyer pays for the next carrier (minority holders know what their shares are worth to a near-monopolist, and a competition authority extracts remedies from a big acquirer it would wave through for a small one) and it draws rivals onto the leader's markets. Keyed on ANY carrier, never on the player specifically — a runaway roll-up meets the same resistance, or this stops being a rule about concentration and becomes a rule about the human.
finance._comment_acquisitionPremium: What an acquirer pays over a target's market cap to take it outright — control costs a premium, ~20-40% in real deals. Also the price a majority owner pays to buy out the minority.
finance._comment_controlThreshold: Stake above which a carrier controls another and may force a full buyout of the rest. Half the shares.
finance._comment_takeoverDefenseChance: Per-quarter chance a raided board actually issues its defensive dilution. Below 1 so a determined raider still makes progress — it just pays for every point of control against a moving target — and so the share count does not balloon every single quarter.
finance._comment_takeoverDefenseThreshold: When an OUTSIDE holder's stake in a carrier reaches this, the carrier's board fights back: it issues equity to dilute the raider (the Railroad Tycoon defence). It slows a takeover to a war of attrition rather than a quiet accumulation, so no one — the player included — quietly ends up owning the whole field. Lower makes carriers defend earlier and takeovers harder.
finance._comment_stakePurchaseCapPerQuarter: The most of a carrier's shares any one buyer may accumulate in a SINGLE quarter, as a fraction of shares outstanding. Building toward a controlling stake therefore takes several quarters — which is the whole point: a raid can be seen coming and defended against, rather than a company changing hands in one click. Modeled on Railroad Tycoon's block-by-block buying. Lower makes takeovers slower and more visible; higher lets a cash-rich raider move fast.
finance._comment_stakeInterestPerQuarter: Per-quarter chance a cash-rich NON-roll-up carrier opens or extends an opportunistic minority stake in a profitable rival — or in the player. This is what makes the share register a live market: legacy, flag and low-cost carriers put surplus cash to work in each other's stock, and a strong player draws real interest in its shares (pillar 4, success attracts sharks). Distinct from the roll-up's control campaigns. Higher = a busier stock market.
finance._comment_stakeCeiling: The most of another carrier an opportunistic (non-roll-up) investor will accumulate — a large minority, held below controlThreshold so it stays an investment and a signal, never a takeover. Only the roll-up pushes a stake past control and folds a target in.
finance._comment_stakeReserveMultiple: How many times its operating reserve a carrier must hold in cash before it puts the surplus into another carrier's stock. Above 1 so a carrier funds its own routes and buffer first and speculates only with genuine surplus — it never starves operations to buy stock.
finance._comment_maxDividend: Ceiling on the dividend a carrier can declare, as a fraction of the quarter's net income. Below 1 so a company can never pay out more than it earns and starve itself in one stroke.
finance._comment_dividendPricePremium: How much a declared dividend lifts the share price: the earnings multiple is scaled by (1 + dividend x this) when the carrier is actually profitable. Raising the dividend visibly lifts the price (income investors pay up), cutting it drops it — the Railroad Tycoon lever, and a real defensive tool against a raider. It only applies to a profitable carrier, so a loss-maker cannot fake a high price with an empty promise. The lift is paid for over time by the cash the payout drains from the balance sheet.
finance._comment_splitPriceThreshold: When a carrier's share price closes a quarter above this, its stock splits (shares and every stake in it multiply, the price divides) until it is back under. Keeps prices legible and is a satisfying sign of success; it changes no one's ownership fraction or the company's value.
finance._comment_splitFactor: How many new shares each old one becomes in a split — 2 for a conventional 2-for-1. Any value above 1 works; the split repeats until the price is back under the threshold.
finance._comment_integration: After an acquisition the combined carrier runs `integrationQuarters` with its operating costs lifted by `integrationDrag` — merging airlines is famously messy. This is the risk that stops acquisitions being free.
finance._comment_hostileSizeMultiple: A rival must be worth at least this many times the player's market cap, and be losing money, before it can be swallowed in a hostile takeover. Being small is not enough — you have to be small AND weak (trailing losses). Let your share price crater and a shark eats you; pillar 5.
finance._comment_hostileGraceTurns: No hostile takeover of the player before this turn (6 years). A startup that has not found its feet is not a takeover target; the threat is for an established carrier that lets itself slide.
finance._comment_craterFraction: The player is a takeover target only once its equity has fallen below this fraction of its own historic peak — the share price has genuinely CRATERED, per pillar 5, not merely stayed modest.
finance._comment_acquisitionMaxTargetFraction: Largest a roll-up will bite, as a fraction of its own market cap. Bolt-ons only — a carrier cannot merge with a near-equal and hand itself the whole field. Keeps consolidation from running to monopoly (pillar/§9: no carrier owns the world).
finance._comment_acquisitionWeakReturn: A carrier is an acquisition target when its trailing-year earnings are below this fraction of its own market cap — an underperformer earning a poor return, or losing money. Set on the TARGET's own return so it never scales with the buyer (which is what caused monopolies). Higher = more carriers in play for M&A; too high and healthy competitors get eaten and the field consolidates.
finance._comment_dealChancePerQuarter: Chance an available deal actually closes in a given quarter. Throttles the M&A RATE independently of how many weak targets exist — real mergers are negotiated over quarters, not struck the instant a target looks cheap. Raise for a livelier M&A scene, lower for a quieter one.
finance._comment_leaseByRating: Multiplier on lease rates by credit rating. A strong balance sheet leases at the base rate; a weak or over-leveraged carrier pays a premium a lessor charges for the risk, up to 50% more at junk. This ties leasing to the finance layer: lever up and your leases get dearer, which brakes the borrow-and-lease-everything strategy.
finance._comment_maxLeaseToEquity: Most annual lease commitments a carrier can carry, as a multiple of its equity. Lessors will not extend unlimited leases against a thin balance sheet — you cannot lease all the aircraft you want, only what your finances support. Binds a carrier trying to grow faster than its equity.
finance._comment_maxBailouts: How many times a carrier can be rescued by a government bailout across all crises. Real airlines got repeated support through COVID, but it is not infinite — keep failing and eventually you fail.
finance._comment_bailoutCushion: Cash a bailout leaves a rescued carrier above zero, booked as debt. Small — a lifeline, not a windfall. The carrier flies on but carries the loan.
finance._comment_maxReorganisations: How many times a carrier may go through Chapter 11 and come back rather than being wound up. ONE. A rival that cannot die is not a rival, it is weather — and on hard about 9.4 carriers fail per game, so an uncapped restructuring turns the whole field into a treadmill. The second failure liquidates. Mirrors maxBailouts, which caps the crisis backstop for the same reason.
finance._comment_reorgDebtKept: Fraction of its debt a carrier still owes after a restructuring. Creditors take the rest — that is what Chapter 11 IS, and a failed rival carries a median $707M of it. The perverse dynamic of the US industry is that this leaves the survivor cheaper than the airlines that never failed.
finance._comment_reorgFleetKept: Fraction of the fleet that survives a restructuring; the rest of the leases are rejected and the metal goes back. Emerging leaner has to COST something or it is a free reset that punishes the player for winning the fare war.
finance._comment_reorgRoutesKept: Fraction of the network that survives, worst sectors dropped first. A restructured airline is a smaller airline.
finance._comment_reorgCostAdvantage: Lasting multiplier on the cost lines a restructured carrier controls — crew, maintenance, ground. Renegotiated contracts and shed obligations really do leave an emerged carrier structurally cheaper, which is the whole point of the mechanic: kill a rival with a fare war and it comes back harder to kill.
finance._comment_reorgCashCushion: USD the carrier emerges holding, as debtor-in-possession financing. Enough to fly, not enough to expand.
finance._comment_distressedQuarters: How long a liquidated carrier's aircraft stay on the market at a discount before the fleet is dispersed.
finance._comment_distressedDiscount: Price of a liquidated carrier's aircraft as a fraction of list. Distressed fleets sell at a steep discount — the estate wants cash and every buyer knows it. This is the reward for having capital when a rival folds.
finance._comment_reorgMinRoutes: Sectors a failing carrier must still fly for a restructuring to be worth attempting. Below it there is no network to reorganise around and the estate is wound up instead — which is the branch that puts aircraft on the distressed market.

entrant._comment: New airlines that spin up mid-game to fill the vacuum consolidation and failure leave — Breeze and Avelo entering the secondary cities the majors abandoned. Keeps the field regenerating rather than only shrinking.
entrant._comment_minTurn: No new startups before this turn (3 years) — the scheduled cast establishes the market first.
entrant._comment_chancePerQuarter: Per-quarter chance a startup enters WHEN the conditions hold (a carrier has left AND at least a third of survivors are profitable AND the field is not full). Tuned to keep the field near its cap — a thinned market draws a new entrant within a year, so failures and consolidation are refilled rather than leaving a sparse world.
entrant._comment_vacuumRoutes: When the rivals between them fly this few routes, the market has collapsed (typically after a scripted crisis in History mode). A startup may then enter to rebuild the market even though nobody is currently profitable — the profitability and vacancy gates are waived. Without this the field cannot recover from a 9/11 or COVID that guts every carrier at once.

scenarios._comment: The two ways to start a game. Present-day is the default 25-year run from today; history is a 50-year run from 2000 with real events and aircraft anchored to their launch dates.

difficulty._comment: Chosen at game start. Each level is a set of multipliers on the baseline (medium = all 1.0, the tuned game). demand scales world traffic on every route (more passengers to win); yield scales the FARE every carrier clears, so it moves margins directly rather than through traffic. demand alone barely touched profitability — because most sectors are capacity-constrained rather than demand-constrained (see docs/demand-audit.md), thinning traffic mostly just reduces the spill nobody was carrying anyway, and hard's median route margin sat at 27.8% against medium's 31.0%. Yield bites where demand does not: it is the same revenue line for everyone, so a thin-margin world punishes a badly-run network without making a well-run one impossible; eventChance scales the RANDOM disaster deck's per-quarter draw (history's SCRIPTED crises are unaffected — they are the point of that scenario); rivalCount scales both the dealt cast size and the live field cap; entrantChance scales how often startups fill vacancies; entryPace scales how fast the dealt cast ARRIVES — it divides both the first entry turn and the gap between entries, and lowers the trailing-profit threshold at which a rival is pulled in early. rivalCount only decides how many rivals a game HAS; without entryPace they all queued up on the same schedule whatever the level, so hard had FEWER rivals on the board at year three than medium (4.2 against 5.3) and nobody had touched the player's markets in 62% of games. Worse, the early-entry trigger keys off player profit, so on a thinner world the player earned less and drew fewer sharks — the pillar-4 accelerator ran BACKWARDS with difficulty; aggression scales every rival's incursion appetite AND how readily it contests the player's own routes AND its loss tolerance; growthActions is how many growth moves a rival may make in ONE quarter — open a sector, raid a market, or add metal to a route it already flies. This is the knob that sets the PACE of the field, and aggression cannot substitute for it: aggression only lowers the bar a move has to clear, so on a thinner world it makes a carrier willing to act on turns it would otherwise skip, while the ceiling of one move per quarter stays put. That is why hard used to expand SLOWER than easy — harsher conditions meant more skipped turns against the same ceiling. Each extra action is re-evaluated against the board the previous one just changed, and stops early on cash or on a move that no longer clears the bar, so a high number buys a fast field rather than a reckless one; Medium went 1 -> 2 on 2026-08-06, and it is the only lever that has ever moved this setting past two standard errors. It was found by changing the QUESTION rather than the knob: medium's headless player was losing 121 games in 240 to takeover against 39 to bankruptcy, so every survival figure quoted for it was mostly measuring a bot that never watches its share register — a way to lose that no competent human ever does. Measured on solvency alone, medium sat at 64% while hard sat at 12%, and hard's losses were 174 bankruptcies to 42 takeovers: hard beats you at running an airline, medium was beating a fixture at reading a cap table. A second growth action a quarter took solvency 64.2% -> 48.1% over 960 games (16 points, SE 4.4) and bankruptcies 88 -> 124. Note 3 is WORSE than 2 and produces FEWER bankruptcies (54 against 64 on the screen): past two moves a quarter the field over-expands, spreads thin and starts killing itself, which eases pressure on the player instead of adding it. Two is where the field contests the player; three is where it contests itself. startingCash scales the PLAYER's opening bank (runway); rivalCapital does the same for every rival's, and the two must move in opposite directions or the setting undercuts itself. Rival capital used to be a flat archetype figure whatever the level, so hard handed rivals no more money while making the world they had to grow in thinner (demand 0.85, yield 0.90) — the field was left UNDER-capitalised on exactly the setting meant to make it fierce, and sometimes never developed at all: measured at turn 25, the largest rival was 73 aircraft in one game and 2 in another. A well-funded field is the difference between rivals that contest a strong player and rivals that never get going; Medium's figure was raised from 1.0 to 1.6 when per-station costs landed: rivals pay to stand up stations like everybody else, which left the field poorer (mean net worth $3.29B -> $2.85B) and medium survival went 57% -> 68% — an easier game, off a change made for realism rather than difficulty. Easy and hard barely moved, because at 0.8 the world is roomy enough not to notice and at 3.2 the field is rich enough not to care; 1.0 was the one setting tight enough for the new cost to bite. This is a recalibration to the world the field now lives in, not a difficulty increase — it restores the game medium already was; Re-measured after the station cost was split into a small one-off plus an ongoing charge, and 1.6 still lands medium at 51% over 120 games (2.0 gives 51% too, 2.4 gives 45%), so it was left alone. Worth knowing why it did not need moving again: an ONGOING station charge is far more balance-neutral than the one-off was, because the player pays it every quarter as well, where the one-off mostly drained the rivals' expansion capital and quietly handed the player the game; stockActivity scales the whole M&A layer — how often rivals buy stakes and open acquisition campaigns, and how low they'll let their cash run to do it, so hard is a feeding frenzy and easy a quiet register; playerFocus scales how much harder a rival is drawn to a market the PLAYER flies than to an equally good one flown by another AI (on top of rivals.json's baseline). Pillar 4 says success attracts sharks, and this is the knob that decides how sharp their teeth are: without it a bigger, faster field simply spreads out over virgin markets and leaves the player alone, which is how hard ended up with BETTER player survival than medium even after the field was made to expand three times as fast; contestPressure scales how hard head-to-head competition bites (it multiplies share.competitionLoadPenalty, the amount rival capacity drags everyone's load factor down), so on hard a contested route empties out and can go unprofitable while on medium it is only a mild dent. Medium's entryPace went 1 -> 1.4 and contestPressure 0.55 -> 0.9 on 2026-08-06, on a player report that it was a bit too easy and after a fifth archetype made it 5 points easier still. The two are SUPERADDITIVE and that is why both moved: alone they measure 49% and 51% survival over 240 games, together 40%. Rivals arriving sooner is only pressure if meeting one hurts, and competition biting harder only matters if somebody has arrived to do it. Medium's yield went 1.0 -> 0.96 on 2026-08-06, after two other levers were tried and failed. entryPace 1.4 -> 2.0 measured 40.0% -> 39.0% over 480 games an arm — nothing, despite genuinely putting a third more rivals on the board by year three (2.8 -> 3.7). Early rivals are small when they land and they also get longer to compound, so the pressure and the payoff cancel. contestPressure is SATURATED above 0.9: 0.9/1.15/1.35 measure 40%/39%/39%, so the 0.55 -> 0.9 step did its work and the lever then stopped. Yield moved it where neither could: 40.0% -> 35.0% over 960 games, a 5-point difference at 1.6 standard errors — suggestive rather than conclusive, and consistent with a separate 240-game screen that showed 6 points the same way. It is the lever this comment already argued for: the same revenue line for everyone, so a thin-margin world punishes a badly-run network without making a well-run one impossible. entryPace is LEFT at 1.4 knowing it buys no difficulty, because a field that arrives sooner is worth having for its own sake — it is texture, not pressure, and it should not be mistaken for pressure by whoever reads this next. Predation was tried first and REJECTED on measurement: turning it on for medium moved survival 53% -> 58%, the wrong way, because a field that undercuts itself grinds its own margins down over a hundred quarters while the player is under no obligation to join in. It remains right for hard, where it is what makes a rival on your route frightening — it is simply not a difficulty lever. Easy: a roomier world with a smaller, gentler field, more cash, a sleepy stock market, and toothless competition. Hard: thinner traffic, a bigger, faster-arriving, more aggressive field that hunts your routes and each other's shares, competition that actually hurts, more disasters and less runway.
difficulty._comment_predation: How ruthless a rival is on a sector it SHARES with somebody: the fraction of that sector's best available profit it will give up in order to price UNDERNEATH the competition rather than sit on the margin. Zero means it simply takes the most profitable posture in its band and ignores who else is there. 0.85 means it will surrender most of the margin to sit at the bottom of its band and squeeze. It only bites where the cheaper fare is still profitable — a rival that prices itself into a loss it cannot fund is not ruthless, it is dead — so squeezing a wolf onto thin margins is what stops it, which is the counterplay. HARD ONLY, on purpose. This was the one axis difficulty did not touch: before it existed, contested sectors on hard were priced at undercut 41.9% of the time against easy's 42.5%, which is to say identically, so meeting a hard rival on a route felt exactly like meeting a gentle one. It is left at zero below hard because the mechanic is SENSITIVE — the notches sit close together in net, so even 0.08 on medium moved its contested mix from 43% undercut to 60% — and medium's balance is tuned. Raise it there only with the harness in hand.
difficulty._comment_contestPressure: How hard being contested bites, as a multiplier on the competition load penalty. Raised on MEDIUM from 0.22 to 0.55 on 2026-08-04: medium had drifted to 64% survival across 120 fixture games against the ~50% it was tuned for, and a player was winning it consistently. Chosen over the alternatives because it is the lever that makes RIVALS the difficulty rather than taxing the player — pillar 4 — and because it only bites on the ~20% of markets that are actually contested, so an uncontested network is unaffected and the change is felt exactly where competition is. Measured 64% -> 52%, with every seed base at or below baseline and the spread tightening from 10-16 to 9-12. NOTE predation was tried first and made medium EASIER (70% -> 75%): a rival that gives up margin to undercut damages itself more than it damages you.
